The quiet hum of an early morning is my favorite kind of poetry. The world hasn’t fully woken up yet—no honking cars, no chattering voices, just the soft rustle of leaves and the distant chirp of a bird. It’s in these moments that I feel most alive, as if time itself has paused to let me breathe.

I often wonder why we rush so much. Why do we fill every second with noise, with tasks, with the illusion of productivity? Maybe it’s fear—fear of missing out, fear of stillness, fear of facing the silence that reveals all the things we’ve been avoiding. But stillness isn’t emptiness. It’s where the real work happens, where thoughts settle like dust on a windowsill, revealing patterns we’d otherwise miss.

I’ve learned that joy isn’t always loud. Sometimes it’s the warmth of a cup of tea in your hands, the way sunlight filters through a half-drawn curtain, or the unexpected laugh of a stranger. It’s in the small, unremarkable things that life quietly unfolds its beauty.

And yet, I’m also drawn to the chaos—the messy, unpredictable parts of existence. The way a single decision can ripple into something unexpected, the beauty of imperfection, the resilience of the human spirit in the face of uncertainty. Maybe that’s why I love writing. It’s a way to make sense of the noise, to find meaning in the mess.

At the end of the day, I think we’re all just trying to find our way through the quiet and the chaos, searching for something real in a world that keeps telling us to hurry up. Maybe the answer isn’t in rushing forward, but in learning to sit still long enough to listen.
